mappings.rationale: Interpret the set-builder condition and enumerate the finite collection it describes.
mappings.answerReason: The positive integers less than 4 are {1,2,3}, which has three elements.

mappings.rationale: Find all positive factors of 12; the set-builder notation supplies the membership condition.
mappings.answerReason: The positive divisors of 12 are 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12, giving six elements.

mappings.rationale: Choose a concise defining condition to represent the infinite collection of all integers.
mappings.answerReason: Set-builder notation gives the exact finite description {x | x is an integer}, supporting D as the intended preference.
limitations: Roster notation with ellipses can also represent all integers, so D is a suitability preference rather than the only valid representation.

mappings.rationale: Read the variable and predicate in set-builder notation as specifying eligible elements.
mappings.answerReason: In {x | x > 0}, x ranges over elements satisfying the condition to the right of the vertical bar.

mappings.rationale: Classify the displayed integers using the explicitly stated convention that natural numbers include zero.
mappings.answerReason: Under the stated convention, 0, 1, and 2 are natural numbers, while −1 is not.

mappings.rationale: All displayed numbers are integers, so identifying the positive ones requires distinguishing positive, negative, and zero.
mappings.answerReason: Only 1 is strictly positive. The numbers −2 and −1 are negative, and 0 is not positive.

mappings.rationale: Determine inclusion between standard number sets and use an irrational number to establish strictness.
mappings.derivedAnswer: A. The rational numbers form a proper subset of the real numbers.
mappings.answerReason: Every rational number is real, but the real number √2 is irrational, so the inclusion is proper.

mappings.rationale: Classify √2 among the standard number sets by recognizing that it is irrational and real.
mappings.answerReason: √2 is an irrational real number, so it belongs to the real numbers but not the rational numbers.

mappings.rationale: Use the definition of a subset to enumerate all eligible sets, including the empty set and itself.
mappings.answerReason: The subsets are ∅, {1}, {2}, and {1,2}, so there are four in total.

mappings.rationale: Determine set equality by comparing membership rather than the order of the written elements.
mappings.derivedAnswer: A. The two sets are equal.
mappings.answerReason: Both sets contain exactly 1 and 2, so each is a subset of the other and they are equal.

mappings.rationale: Apply the subset definition to the empty set and identify its sole possible subset.
mappings.answerReason: A subset of ∅ cannot contain any element, so it must be ∅ itself. Thus there is one subset.

mappings.rationale: Translate the subset relation directly into a statement about every element of the smaller set.
mappings.derivedAnswer: C. Every element of A is in B.
mappings.answerReason: A ⊆ B means that membership in A implies membership in B; equality is allowed.

mappings.rationale: Count all subsets of a three-element set, then exclude the set itself to obtain proper subsets.
mappings.answerReason: There are 2³ = 8 subsets, and exactly one is the entire set, leaving 8 − 1 = 7 proper subsets.

mappings.rationale: Distinguish proper subsets from all subsets of a singleton.
mappings.answerReason: The subsets of {1} are ∅ and {1}; only ∅ is proper, giving one proper subset.

mappings.rationale: Use the defining inequality between a proper subset and its containing set.
mappings.answerReason: A proper subset must be different from the containing set, so no set is a proper subset of itself.

mappings.rationale: Apply the finite proper-subset count by excluding the whole set from all subsets.
mappings.answerReason: A four-element set has 2⁴ = 16 subsets. Removing the set itself leaves 15 proper subsets.

mappings.rationale: Find the elements common to both finite sets and count the intersection.
mappings.answerReason: The common elements are 3 and 4, so A ∩ B = {3,4} has two elements.

mappings.rationale: Recognize that an intersection is empty when the sets have no common elements.
mappings.answerReason: Neither 1 nor 2 belongs to {3,4}, so the intersection is ∅ and contains zero elements.

mappings.rationale: Apply the intersection definition when both operands are the same set.
mappings.answerReason: Every element of A belongs to both copies of A, so A ∩ A = A = {1,2,3}, with three elements.

mappings.rationale: Use the subset condition to determine which elements satisfy membership in both sets.
mappings.answerReason: Since every element of A is already in B, precisely the elements of A belong to both sets.

mappings.rationale: Compute a two-set union count by subtracting the overlap counted twice.
Combine the elements of both finite sets without counting a shared element twice.
mappings.answerReason: A ∪ B = {1,2,3,4}; the shared element 2 is included only once, giving four elements.

mappings.rationale: Use containment to recognize that adjoining B contributes no new elements to A.
mappings.answerReason: Because B ⊆ A, the union A ∪ B equals A and therefore has five elements.

mappings.rationale: Relate membership in either operand to membership in its union.
mappings.derivedAnswer: B. A is a subset of A ∪ B.
mappings.answerReason: Every element of A satisfies the union condition of belonging to A or B, so A ⊆ A ∪ B.

mappings.rationale: Find a complement's cardinality by removing the subset's elements from the finite universal set.
mappings.answerReason: The complement contains the universal set's elements outside A, so its size is 5 − 2 = 3.

mappings.rationale: Identify the elements of the specified universe that are absent from A.
mappings.answerReason: Removing 1 and 4 from U leaves the complement {2,3}, which has two elements.

mappings.rationale: Apply the supplied cardinality preservation for taking a complement twice.
mappings.answerReason: Taking complements twice in the same universe returns A, so the resulting cardinality is |A| = 6.
limitations: The stem already supplies cardinality preservation, so no derivation of the double-complement rule is required.

mappings.rationale: Use the defining disjointness of a set and its complement.
mappings.answerReason: No element can both belong to A and lie outside A, so A ∩ Aᶜ = ∅.

mappings.rationale: Only the union count is requested, so use the two-set overlap formula.
mappings.answerReason: |A ∪ B| = 5 + 4 − 2 = 7; the universal-set size is not needed for this calculation.

mappings.rationale: Combine a union cardinality calculation with complementation in the specified finite universe.
mappings.answerReason: First |A ∪ B| = 5 + 4 − 2 = 7. Its complement therefore has 8 − 7 = 1 element.

mappings.rationale: Within A, the requested elements form the complement of A ∩ B relative to A.
mappings.answerReason: A splits into the two shared elements and those outside B, so |A \ B| = 6 − 2 = 4.

mappings.rationale: Compare two orders of intersection and complementation by evaluating a finite counterexample.
mappings.derivedAnswer: D. They are not necessarily the same.
mappings.answerReason: Let U = {1,2}, A = {1}, and B = {2}. Then Aᶜ ∩ Bᶜ = ∅, whereas (A ∩ B)ᶜ = U.
